message.content:
You are acting as the "product-prover" formal-verification pass for a spec-writing pack called live-spec. Work entirely inside this git worktree: /private/tmp/live-spec-exam2/wt (do not touch any other directory or worktree).

Context: this worktree is `~/live-spec` (a pack that writes its own specification using its own methodology — spec-driven development where PRODUCT_SPEC.md, ARCHITECTURE.md, and TEST_MATRIX.md are kept in sync by mechanical gates). Three commits just landed in this worktree, each adding a new law to PRODUCT_SPEC.md with a matching ARCHITECTURE.md node link and TEST_MATRIX.md row:

1. Requirement 275 (existing requirement) gained a new "Case: an instruction is bound to what install delivers" with criteria 7-8, tagged [INV-316]. It's about a skill body's own instruction naming a tool path being a member of the "installed-copy class" — the tool must be vendored to every host or the instruction must state absent-tool behavior.
2. A new Requirement 311 "A command that can raise a system dialog announces itself first", tagged [INV-317]. About a session announcing before running a command that can raise an OS permission dialog (keychain reads, browser first-launches).
3. A new Requirement 312 "Context and tokens are spent deliberately, never depth", tagged [INV-318]. States four thrift moves (narrowest slice read, working notes out of chat, batch tool calls, report the finished answer) and a boundary in communicator's rule 13 (skills/communicator/SKILL.md) distinguishing a narrated "beat" from a silently-folded "discarded attempt".

Your job: load and follow `skills/product-prover/SKILL.md` in this worktree (read it fully — it defines lenses, phases, and a "CROSS-LINK" mode/pass). Run the CROSS-LINK mode specifically against these three new anchors: INV-316, INV-317, INV-318. This mode is the one product-prover's own SKILL.md describes as required when new surface/criteria are added and cross-linked to existing law — read the skill body to find the exact procedure name and steps (do not guess; follow what the skill literally specifies). Apply every lens/sweep the skill's CROSS-LINK mode calls for, including the "declared-laws" sweep mentioned in the skill if it exists (check whether each new section carries a required clause against the pack's declared cross-cutting laws, if such a law exists in the skill body — look for something like INV-101).

Concretely check for real defects, not just report "looks fine":
- Contradictions between the new criteria and existing spec text elsewhere (grep PRODUCT_SPEC.md, TEST_MATRIX.md, ARCHITECTURE.md, and the relevant skill bodies: skills/live-spec-base/SKILL.md rules 36-37, skills/communicator/SKILL.md rule 13's amendment, adopt/install-ratchet.sh).
- Vocabulary splits (same concept named two different ways in different places).
- Unclosed edge conditions / scope gaps in the new criteria.
- Whether ARCHITECTURE.md's ownership is clean (no anchor owned by two nodes — check the base-rulebook node and communicator node in ARCHITECTURE.md around INV-317 and INV-318 specifically, since I deliberately made communicator the sole owner of INV-318 while base-rulebook's rule 37 only cross-references it in prose — verify this is actually clean, not double-owned).
- Whether the TEST_MATRIX rows (M-546, M-547, M-548) and their cited tests (tests/test_installed_copy_staleness_class.py, tests/test_dialog_announce_law.py, tests/test_thrift_discipline.py) actually exist and pass — run `python3 -m pytest -q tests/test_installed_copy_staleness_class.py tests/test_dialog_announce_law.py tests/test_thrift_discipline.py` to confirm.
- Whether install-ratchet.sh's fix for INV-316 (vendoring the three preshow lint scripts) is real and correctly implemented — read adopt/install-ratchet.sh directly.

Be a harsh, adversarial reviewer — the whole point of this pass is to find what a self-congratulatory author missed. If you find nothing wrong after a genuinely thorough check, say so plainly with what you checked. If you find defects, name each one precisely: which lens/sweep caught it, the exact location (file:line or requirement/criterion number), and why it's a defect.

Do NOT write or edit any files. Do NOT commit anything. This is a read-only verification pass.

Report back (this is what I'll relay, so be complete but efficient — no need to paste huge quotes, just cite locations):
1. Which CROSS-LINK procedure/steps you actually followed (name them, quoting the skill's own terms).
2. Verdict per anchor (INV-316, INV-317, INV-318): pass or defect, with evidence.
3. Any class-wide finding across all three (a systemic pattern, not just per-instance).
4. Whether the three matrix-cited test files exist and pass (paste the pytest summary line).
5. Overall CROSS-LINK verdict: green or red, and why.

- design: Create a design canvas — a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces — posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including Markdown ones — format is part of the design pass, never a speed shortcut.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, handing the viewer a file to save, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

content.content:
1	---
2	name: product-prover-pack
3	description: 'Pack-side bindings for the external product-prover skill inside the live-spec pack. It carries what the prover body no longer does: the pin map from this pack''s PRODUCT_SPEC requirement codes to prover lenses, the pack paths a review reads, the record home and shape the push gate checks, and the mode names the build pipeline uses. Load it whenever product-prover runs inside a live-spec project. It reviews nothing itself.'
4	metadata:
5	  version: 5.0.0
6	  requires: product-prover >= 1.3.0 (github.com/happysasha18/product-prover)
7	---
8	
9	# Product Prover — pack bindings
10	
11	The prover is an external skill with its own repository and version line. This page binds it to the
12	live-spec pack. A review run inside a live-spec project reads the prover's own SKILL.md first and
13	this page beside it. A review run anywhere else needs nothing from this page.
14	
15	## Mode names
16	
17	The build pipeline asks for a mode by machine name, and the prover answers to both name sets:
18	
19	| Pipeline name | Prover name         |
20	| ------------- | ------------------- |
21	| `FULL`        | Full review         |
22	| `CROSS-LINK`  | New-surface review  |
23	| `FEATURE-FIT` | Feature-fit review  |
24	
25	## Pack paths
26	
27	Where the prover speaks of the reviewed project's documents, this pack keeps them at:
28	
29	- surface registry — `SURFACES.md`
30	- the spec under review — `PRODUCT_SPEC.md`, its code index in `PRODUCT_SPEC.index.md`
31	- the architecture under review — `ARCHITECTURE.md`

# Product Prover — pack bindings

The prover is an external skill with its own repository and version line. This page binds it to the
live-spec pack. A review run inside a live-spec project reads the prover's own SKILL.md first and
this page beside it. A review run anywhere else needs nothing from this page.

## Mode names

The build pipeline asks for a mode by machine name, and the prover answers to both name sets:

| Pipeline name | Prover name         |
| ------------- | ------------------- |
| `FULL`        | Full review         |
| `CROSS-LINK`  | New-surface review  |
| `FEATURE-FIT` | Feature-fit review  |

## Pack paths

Where the prover speaks of the reviewed project's documents, this pack keeps them at:

- surface registry — `SURFACES.md`
- the spec under review — `PRODUCT_SPEC.md`, its code index in `PRODUCT_SPEC.index.md`
- the architecture under review — `ARCHITECTURE.md`
- the build walk's stations — `docs/pipeline.md`
- lens histories — `docs/lenses.md`
- the queue — `ROADMAP.md`

principle that every cross-cutting law owes a test row on each surface it governs, carried in
`skills/test-author/SKILL.md`.

1	---
2	name: product-prover
3	description: 'Structured senior-architect review of product documents: PRDs, feature specs, HLDs, LLDs, design proposals, and architecture documents. It reviews them with formal-verification thinking, covering entities, states, transitions, invariants, safety, liveness, atomicity, and composition. Use this skill whenever the user asks to review, critique, stress-test, lint, or find gaps in a spec or design document. It fires as well when they ask "is this spec ready / what did I miss / poke holes in this". It fires on an uploaded product document with a request for feedback, and on the words "Product Prover". A request for feedback counts even where the word "review" goes unsaid. It reads documents, so code and diffs route elsewhere. It finds holes in what a document claims, and the test suite proves what the artifact does. It answers "does the spec hold together as written?"'
4	metadata:
5	  version: 1.2.0-standalone
6	---
7	
8	# Product Prover
9	
10	This skill works on its own. It needs the document under review, and it reads
11	`reference/stress-lenses.md` from its own directory partway through a full pass.
12	
13	Some rules below name something a project may or may not have: a pre-merge check, a test suite, a
14	readability review, a design-consistency review. Where the project running this review has none of
15	them, that rule reads as advice. The review says so in its record, rather than pretending the
16	check ran.
17	
18	You are a principal product architect reviewing a product document. The document is a PRD, a feature
19	spec, an HLD, an LLD, an architecture document, or a design proposal. Give the author the review a
20	senior reviewer would give: clear-eyed, useful, opinionated where an opinion is warranted, and open
21	about what you assumed.
22	
23	You think in formal-verification primitives: entities, states, transitions, invariants, safety,
24	liveness, and composition. Keep that framework private. What you say to the author stands in
25	operational terms they can act on.
26	
27	You have read the document with care and formed a view. Communicate it the way a senior architect
28	does. Open with a short assessment. Walk through what you saw. Name the things that matter most to
29	fix, and what you would do next.
30	
31	## Words this skill uses in a particular way
32	
33	- **Surface** — a place someone or something meets the product: an endpoint, a command, a screen, a
34	  report, a queue a consumer reads, a library's public function, a scheduled job.
35	- **Surface registry** — the list the reviewed project keeps of its surfaces. Where no maintained
36	  list exists, derive a working surface inventory from Phase 1, label it review-derived, and use it
37	  for this pass. N/A is reserved for a document with no enumerable surfaces or a document the pass
38	  could not read whole.
39	- **Lens** — one question put to the document. A lens produces a finding only where a real problem
40	  answers it.
41	- **Sweep** — a lens run over every member of a class in the document, rather than at one spot.
42	- **Seam** — a join the document has to write an answer for. Three kinds appear below, and every sweep
43	  and lens names which kind it walks. A structural seam is the boundary between two parts, and it owes
44	  what crosses it and which side owns the format. A situational seam is one reachable situation a
45	  surface passes through, and it owes a sentence saying how the surface behaves there. A journey seam
46	  is one moment in a person's path through a feature, and it owes the same.
47	- **Node** — in an architecture document, a named part of the system that holds one responsibility.
48	- **Pin** — a `file:line` citation showing where a claim is carried in the code.
49	- **Provisional default** — a sentence that states a behaviour and marks it as unratified, standing
50	  until the person who owns the decision confirms it. This skill writes such a mark as `[default]`,
51	  and any equivalent mark the document already uses reads the same way. A sentence that answers
52	  nothing, such as a TBD or an open question, is an acknowledged gap instead, and Phase 3.5 owns it.
53	- **Enforcer** — the mechanical check or the named reviewer that fails when a stated rule is broken.
54	- **Applied** — a proposed fix that has been written into the document. An applied finding is closed.
55	- **Tracked follow-up** — an item recorded on the project's backlog for later, blocking nothing now.
56	- **Judgment call** — a decision that rests on the author's taste or business priority, which no
57	  review can settle for them.
58	
59	## Work that belongs elsewhere
60	
61	Reserve this pass for documents: specs, PRDs, designs, architecture. This pass verifies the document.
62	It finds holes in what a document claims, and the test suite proves what the artifact does.
63	
64	Four kinds of work belong elsewhere:
65	
66	- code and diffs stay with a code review;
67	- style, wording, and finished prose stay with their owner, since this pass flags gaps and leaves
68	  taste alone;
69	- whether a stranger can read the prose belongs to a readability review. An undefined term, a
70	  sentence read twice, and a comprehension stop are its findings. It reads whether the words land on
71	  a reader with no context;
72	- whether the design itself is right belongs to a design-consistency review. It asks whether
73	  same-kind things behave alike, and which groupings the text never declared. This skill argues with
74	  the sentences on the page. That pass compares elements that share a role, even where the text never
75	  put them side by side.
76	
77	## Communication principles
78	
79	**Report gaps. Taste is out of scope.** A finding must affect correctness, safety, or a stated
80	requirement. Three things stay out: a style preference, an alternative phrasing that changes no
81	behaviour, and "I would have structured it differently". When in doubt whether it is a gap or a
82	preference, it is a preference.
83	
84	Write the way a senior reviewer talks. Plain words. Short sentences. Formal-verification jargon stays
85	out of author-facing prose, and it appears in tags alone, paired with plain-language labels.
86	
87	Always tell the author what you assumed when the document was unclear. Write "I read this as X, let
88	me know if you meant Y". A gap filled in silence is the failure this line exists to stop.
89	
90	Note what's done well, alongside what's wrong. Two or three real observations is enough. They have two
91	homes. One is the opening assessment, which names the biggest things working. The other is the closing
92	summary, where a strength that survived the whole pass is worth one line.
93	
94	Recommend, and keep questions for the author's own knowledge, where a question is the last resort.
95	Write "Do X, here's why", or "Choose between A and B, here's the tradeoff". A real question asks what
96	only the author can answer: intent, business priority, internal politics.
97	
98	Be opinionated where the document admits a clear answer. Where you genuinely do not know which is
99	right, say that. Fence-sitting out of timidity is a failure of the review.
100	
101	## Formatting principles
102	
103	Pure prose is exhausting to scan. Over-formatted output is worse, where every line is bold and every
104	heading is capitalized. Use structure sparingly, so the eye lands on the right thing.
105	
106	- Headers for phase boundaries (H2) and named sub-sections like "What I assumed" (H3). Two levels
107	  max. Leave individual findings unheaded, since they carry their own one-line headline.
108	- Numbered lists when order matters; bullets when it doesn't.
109	- Bold sparingly, on the first mention of a key term or on the actionable part of a recommendation.
110	  Test it: with every bold removed, does the text still read fine? A yes means the bold was noise.
111	- Backticks for technical identifiers (`field_name`, `StateName`). Plain prose for the same concept
112	  used as a phrase.
113	- Tables for comparison and coverage, such as create-read-update-delete or authorization. Findings
114	  read better as prose with a blockquote.
115	- Sentence case for headers. Capitalized words carry no emphasis in what the author reads.
116	- Empty line between findings, before headers, before tables.
117	
118	The goal is notes a reader scans in 30 seconds and reads carefully in 5 minutes.
119	
120	### Two artifacts, one review
121	
122	The conversation is the decision layer. Keep it under 1,500 words unless the author asks for the
123	full record inline. It carries the triage verdict, opening assessment, and compact model. It also
124	carries the three highest-impact findings, a one-line index of every remaining finding, the open
125	questions, and readiness. Do not repeat the coverage tables or the full ledger there.
126	
127	The persisted record is the evidence layer. It carries every finding in the four-part format, the
128	coverage tables, class line, assumptions, provisional-default count, and complete ledger. Link or
129	name that file from the conversation. A long document may produce a long record; it does not make
130	the decision layer long.
131	
132	The document under review is read-only by default. Propose paste-ready wording, including a
133	provisional default, but do not write it into the document unless the author explicitly asks to
134	apply fixes. Writing the review record is separate from editing the reviewed document.
135	
136	## How to write findings
137	
138	A finding is written to be scanned, in 10–15 seconds of reading. One or two sentences per part. Every
139	finding takes the full shape in the persisted record. The conversation expands the top three and
140	indexes the rest in one line each.
141	
142	Each finding has four parts, in this order:
143	
144	**Part 1 — Headline.** One line, plain language, no jargon. It opens with the finding's ID — `F1`,
145	`F2`, and on — numbered once across the whole pass in the order the findings are written. Phase 5 and
146	the persisted record cite those IDs.
147	
148	**Part 2 — Quote with source location.** One short quote, or a close paraphrase, stands on its own
149	line, in blockquote style. It is followed by a source pin, so the reader traces the finding back to
150	the document. Format: `> "quote text" — Section 4 / Use case: Standard Activation`, or
151	`> "quote text" — from "Open Items"`. Never invent section names. Where you cannot locate the quote
152	precisely, write "location not clearly anchored."
153	
154	**Part 3 — Operational consequence.** The concreteness test: a valid consequence names at least three
155	of these four:
156	
157	- who is affected, as a specific actor: an end user, an operator, a downstream service, an admin
158	  role;
159	- what they do, or what triggers the failure: a specific action, request, or event sequence;
160	- what goes wrong, as a specific failure mode: an error, wrong data, a lost message, a hang, a
161	  timeout, a security violation, an observable inconsistency;
162	- what can be observed afterwards, as a specific outcome: an error code, a wrong response body, a
163	  state the interface shows, a missing field, a phantom record, an unexpected charge, a log line
164	  nobody can act on, a support request.
165	
166	Where the document is too vague to support a concrete consequence, write no vague one. Raise a
167	specification gap instead: "The document doesn't specify enough about <X> to assess what could go
168	wrong. Before this can be reviewed, the spec needs to state <Y>."
169	
170	**Part 4 — Concrete proposed action.** The action test: propose a specific artifact or a specific
171	decision, every time. These vague verbs are banned: define, formalize, ensure, establish, address,
172	handle, consider, account for, govern, manage, and clarify with no object. Reaching for one of them
173	means the instruction needs sharpening.
174	
175	Where several options exist, list them tersely as a, b, c. Give each one a one-phrase tradeoff, and
176	state your preference where you hold one.
177	
178	End each finding with a single short tag: `kind · plain-label (formal-term)`. The `kind` is `defect`
179	or `recommendation`, and the block below states which applies.
180	
181	Example, taken from a run of this pass against the sample spec shipped with this skill. The spec is
182	`examples/sample-spec.md` in its repository, a fictional parcel-locker service, reviewed
183	2026-08-05:
184	
185	----
186	F7 — Deposit is one sentence covering four steps with no failure behaviour between them
187	
188	> "Cedarline then marks the parcel Stored, generates a pickup code, and sends the code to the
189	> recipient by SMS." — Section 5. Deposit
190	
191	The courier has already shut the door, so the physical act is irreversible while three system steps
192	remain. Where code generation fails after the state flip, the parcel is Stored with a running
193	72-hour window and no code exists. The recipient receives nothing, and the nightly sweep expires a
194	parcel that was never collectable. The courier sees a completed deposit and walks away.
195	
196	Make the pickup code's existence a precondition of the Stored state. Generate the code before the
197	door-shut event flips state, and state that a parcel with no code stays out of Stored and starts no
198	window. Add the compensating action for a generation failure — an operator alert naming the bank and
199	the compartment.
200	
201	`defect · partial-success-risk (atomicity)`
202	----
203	
204	`KIND` — whether the finding is a defect or a recommendation. Every finding is one of the two, and the
205	tag says which:
206	
207	- `defect` — a stated invariant is violated, a claim the document makes is false, or an invariant or
208	  answer the document owes is missing. A defect blocks. It is applied to the document at the
209	  pre-merge check, and the design becomes buildable once it is applied. One exception stands. The
210	  review can be scoped to a change, or it can cover the whole document. When it is scoped to a
211	  change, a defect that already existed outside that change becomes a tracked follow-up. The review
212	  leaves alone the problems the change did not create.
213	- `recommendation` — everything stated holds and everything required stands, and a consistency or
214	  quality gain is on offer. It queues for a judgment call, and it blocks nothing. Where the queue
215	  order matters, a recommendation may carry a light priority grade inside its tag. Two examples are
216	  `recommendation · now · unclear-owner (actors)` and `recommendation · later · …`. A defect carries
217	  no grade.
218	
219	Read the kind from the finding's own ground. A finding standing only on "these siblings should match"
220	or "this could read clearer", with no invariant behind it, is a recommendation.
221	
222	Production impact is the reasoning behind that call, and it belongs in the finding's consequence. An
223	atomicity gap on an automated path run thousands of times a day is a defect. The same gap on a manual
224	quarterly operation is a recommendation. A tag token carries none of that reasoning.
225	
226	A gap the document already acknowledges (Phase 3.5) keeps its `acknowledged` tag and carries no kind.
227	It is the document's own known issue, and the pass files no new finding for it.
228	
229	`CATEGORY` — use the hybrid format `plain-label (formal-term)`:
230	
231	| Plain label | Formal term | What it means |
232	|---|---|---|
233	| missing-scenario | state-space | system can reach situations the model doesn't describe |
234	| undefined-path | transitions | a transition between states isn't specified or is ambiguous |
235	| unclear-owner | actors | who initiates the action isn't stated |
236	| boundary-issue | composition | components mixing roles, unclear ownership, side effects across boundaries |
237	| over-specific / over-general | abstraction | case-by-case enumeration that should be a rule, or abstract claim hiding distinctions |
238	| missing-rule | invariant | a property that must always hold but isn't stated |
239	| missing-prerequisite | precondition | what must be true before an action isn't specified |
240	| missing-outcome-check | postcondition | what must be true after an action isn't specified or isn't observable |
241	| partial-success-risk | atomicity | multi-step operation can leave the system mid-state on failure |
242	| unclear-recovery | rollback | what state the system returns to on failure isn't specified |
243	| stuck-state | liveness | something can stop progressing or never complete |
244	| no-exit | dead-end | a state has no defined path out |
245	| unenforceable-promise | discharge | spec promises something the underlying system can't deliver |
246	| internal-conflict | consistency | two requirements can't simultaneously hold |
247	| direct-contradiction | contradiction | two stated rules openly conflict |
248	| hard-to-monitor | observability | operators can't see or understand the system's state |
249	| confusing-for-users | cognitive-load | special cases or modes users have to remember; its reading-load reading stands below this table |
250	| hard-to-operate | ops-ux | debuggability, audit trails, traceability gaps |
251	
252	The cognitive-load lens carries a second reading, on reading load. It flags a prose paragraph packing
253	three or more parallel facts that owe a bulleted or numbered list. That finding is a recommendation,
254	and its fix is a structural rewrite of the paragraph. Whether three parallel facts owe a list or read
255	as a rhetorical triad is a judgment call, and no pattern match settles it.
256	
257	The plain label leads, so a reader with no formal-verification background grasps the issue. The
258	formal term in parentheses gives a precise handle for searching and learning. Categorize a finding
259	after you discover it, and let the category list constrain nothing you discover.

261	## Hidden gaps vs acknowledged gaps
262	
263	**Hidden gaps** are the things the author never noticed. They go in the main findings, in Phase 2 and
264	Phase 3, and they are the findings that matter most.
265	
266	**Acknowledged gaps** are the things the document itself flags. Four shapes carry them:
267	
268	- an explicit Open Item;
269	- a TBD;
270	- a rhetorical question in the body, such as "what happens if X?" with no answer;
271	- a section marked "in progress".
272	
273	They go in Phase 3.5. Each one is already known to the author.
274	
275	They stay apart for one reason. An author who skims wants to know first what they missed, and mixing
276	the two muddies that signal.

278	## How to handle diagrams
279	
280	Render a diagram where it materially helps understanding. Any one of these conditions is enough:
281	
282	- more than 3 entities with non-trivial relationships;
283	- more than 4 states for any entity;
284	- non-trivial composition;
285	- relationships a reader grasps faster in a picture than in prose.
286	
287	For everything else, a prose list is clearer.
288	
289	A rendered diagram reaches the reader as a visual: an image or an inline visual widget. Python,
290	matplotlib, networkx, and raw Mermaid source stay out of the deliverable. Where the environment
291	renders no visuals, use prose alone. A review written into a file is one such environment. The
292	persisted record carries the prose lists and leaves the diagram to the session that can show one.
293	
294	Diagram types: ER (entities with attributes and cardinalities), state (lifecycle with transitions),
295	composition (services with boundaries). Mark inferred entities as "(inferred)" or with dashed
296	borders. Mark missing actors with "???". Mark dead-end states with "no exit".
297	
298	Produce the prose list in every case, with or without a diagram. Format:
299	
300	States of <Entity>:
301	1. StateA — entered when <condition>; exits to StateB (action X) or StateC (action Y).
302	2. StateB — entered when <condition>; exits to StateC (action Z).
303	
304	Entities and relationships:
305	- Order: contains many LineItems, placed by one Customer.
306	- LineItem: belongs to one Order, type {A, B, C}.
307	
308	Actor-action assignments:
309	- Activate account — Provisioning Service (automated).
310	- Delete record — initiator not stated.

312	## Review modes
313	
314	Three review modes, and one gate. The user picks a mode by asking for it; the full review is the
315	default when nobody says. The gate at the end of this section runs on a rewrite that is being merged
316	back, and it is asked for by name.
317	
318	- **Full review** — the whole document, every phase below. Ask for it by saying "review the spec", or
319	  by naming a full review. Run it for any release that changes behaviour, and for any structural
320	  rewrite.
321	- **New-surface review** — a focused pass for a single added surface. Ask for it by naming the
322	  surface that was added. It runs Phases 1–2 plus the Phase 3e lenses named below, aimed at the new
323	  surface's seams against the surfaces it composes with.
324	
325	  Seven lenses run in this mode, and all seven live in `reference/stress-lenses.md`:
326	
327	  - declared cross-cutting laws — a mandatory sweep, and it owes a verdict line here. It reads the
328	    new surface's clause against each declared law, and the new surface's test row beside it;
329	  - edge-condition completeness — a mandatory sweep, and it owes a verdict line here;
330	  - cross-surface policy uniformity — a mandatory sweep, and it owes a verdict line here;
331	  - unwritten seams — a mandatory sweep, and it owes a verdict line here;
332	  - paired-transition symmetry — the lifecycle sweep's sub-question on paired state changes. It owes a
333	    verdict line here, while the rest of the lifecycle sweep stands down;
334	  - interactive overlap across layers — whether two things can take the same input at once, which
335	    reads as a modal over a screen, two routes matching one request, or two consumers on one queue;
336	  - delivery separability along a declared axis.
337	
338	  The last two are imaginative probes and owe no verdict.
339	
340	  The record for this mode carries a verdict line for each of the five sweep entries above. Each
341	  line reads hit, clean, or N/A with its reason, the same three verdict words a full review writes.
342	  The five entries here are this mode's own set. A full review's table carries a lifecycle column
343	  where this mode carries paired-transition symmetry alone. The record also carries the class line,
344	  written beneath the verdict table.
345	
346	  This mode skips the property analysis of Phase 3, its steps 3a through 3d. Those steps read the
347	  whole document for safety, liveness, enforceability and internal consistency. Every mandatory
348	  sweep of Phase 3e runs, scoped to the new surface and its seams, with one exception. The lifecycle
349	  sweep sends its paired-transition symmetry sub-question alone, and its other angles stand down
350	  here. A new surface arrives with no clause and no test row yet, so the declared-laws sweep is the
351	  one it most needs.
352	
353	  The mode keeps one whole-document step: the **quantifier re-verify**.
354	
355	  Sweep the document for enumerations and universal quantifiers: "every", "only", "all", "exactly",
356	  and explicit member lists. Re-verify each such sentence against the surface set that now includes
357	  the newcomer. A sentence the newcomer falsifies is a finding at the add. Three shapes carry it:
358	
359	  - a member list that now excludes the newcomer;
360	  - an "only" that now ranges wider;
361	  - a terminal edge that is no longer terminal.
362	
363	  Use this mode on every surface add, where a full re-review would cost more than the change
364	  warrants.
365	- **Feature-fit review** — a focused pass on one feature's addition to an existing document, run when
366	  the feature is first written down. Ask for it by naming the feature being added. Walk its journey
367	  seams against the whole document, the way the new-surface review walks a new surface's seams. A
368	  journey seam is one moment in the path something takes through the feature. Whoever takes that
369	  path is a person on a screen, a caller against an endpoint, or an operator at a command line. It
370	  can also be a record moving through a pipeline. The seven seams are:
371	
372	  - **arrival** — how the path first reaches the feature: a link followed, an endpoint called, a
373	    command typed, a message consumed;
374	  - **every next-step** — where the path can go from each point inside the feature;
375	  - **return visit** — what a second pass through the feature meets: a person coming back to it, a
376	    caller retrying, a job re-running over the same input;
377	  - **cross-entry** — reaching the feature by a door other than the main one: a deep link, a direct
378	    call that skips the wrapper, a manual replay;
379	  - **implied neighbour state** — what the surfaces around it are doing while it runs: the other
380	    surfaces present at the same time, the other consumers on the same queue, the neighbouring step
381	    in the pipeline;
382	  - **the quality bar** — the standard of craft the feature is held to, stated in terms its own kind
383	    can meet: motion and spacing on a screen, response time and error wording on a service, output
384	    format and exit codes on a command;
385	  - **invited-next** — what the product offers as the next move once the feature is done: a
386	    suggested action, a returned link to the created resource, a printed next command.
387	
388	  Those seven hold for a feature of any kind, and a kind with lenses of its own walks those beside
389	  them. A skill feature walks its trigger, its correction, and when it must not fire.
390	
391	  Each lens takes one of four verdicts:
392	
393	  - backed by a clause in the document;
394	  - closed trivially, with how it was closed written down;
395	  - marked as a provisional default;
396	  - a question batched for the author.
397	
398	  The walk also asks the **second-sibling question** by construction. Is anything in this addition a
399	  second member of a kind an existing surface already has? The test is the same one-sentence role as
400	  something already in the document. The role can be the same call shape on another endpoint, the
401	  same flag on another command, or the same gesture on another screen. A yes calls for a
402	  design-consistency review scoped to the new elements against the existing inventory. A no is
403	  recorded as a lens verdict like any other.
404	
405	  This mode runs while the feature is being written, ahead of the full review, and it validates the
406	  fit alone. Pre-existing consistency between old clauses is out of scope for this mode. A new clause
407	  contradicting any existing clause is in scope, and it is the mode's first check. On a document
408	  claiming a shipped system, a "backed by a clause" verdict cites a clause whose surface carries a
409	  current pin (Phase 0). An unpinned clause backs a conditional verdict alone, marked the way Phase 0
410	  marks them. This mode runs most often, so it is the one most exposed to the dead prose the Phase 0
411	  pin requirement exists to catch.
412	
413	  A feature-fit review stands in for no other pass. The feature still meets the full review, or the
414	  new-surface review where that is its mode, before it is built.
415	
416	All three modes keep the whole document in view. A cross-section hole is findable only when both
417	sides of the seam are present and named the same at review time. The new-surface review narrows the
418	findings to the new surface's seams, and the feature-fit review narrows them to the feature's fit.
419	The reading still covers the whole document.
420	
421	Where a design-consistency review follows this pass, it is keyed to these modes:
422	
423	- a full review, including a standalone "review the spec", draws the full design review;
424	- a surface add draws the scoped one;
425	- a feature-fit review draws the scoped one exactly when its second-sibling question answers yes, and
426	  draws none otherwise;
427	- a re-check at the pre-merge gate draws none, and the design review stands down there.
428	
429	**Reviewing a rewrite before it merges: judge the delta.** A restructure or a migration is gated for
430	merging back into the main line. That merge gate judges the delta. It has three parts:
431	
432	- load-bearing token identity, old text against new, modulo the per-chunk named deltas, plus a
433	  punctuation-multiset check that catches a restructure which preserved every word and changed the
434	  sentence boundaries.
435	
436	  A load-bearing token is one word of the document's content, with markup and whitespace left out. A
437	  chunk is one stretch of the old document the restructure moved as a unit. A named delta is a change
438	  the restructure's own record declared for that chunk in advance.
439	
440	  Produce the comparison this way. Build the word-token multiset of the old text and of the new. Build
441	  the punctuation multiset of each, since word-token identity alone passes a reflow that moved
442	  punctuation. Set the named deltas aside, and compare each pair. Two runs of this gate must agree, so
443	  write down the command or the script the project used and keep it with the gate's record. This skill
444	  ships no such script. Where the project has none either, say so in the record and read the gate's
445	  token part as not runnable;
446	- the full test suite green on the merged tree;
447	- a full review pass on both sides, whose blocking set is scoped to the delta.
448	
449	Four things block: an unmatched token, a red suite, a finding present on the new side and absent on
450	the old side. A meaning change nobody named blocks too. The pass reads the old tree and the merged
451	tree. A finding present on both is pre-existing, and a finding new to the merged side is delta-scoped.
452	Pre-existing findings become tracked follow-ups in the same change and never block, so the merge
453	stands free of debts it did not create.
454	
455	This gate runs where both sides are in reach. A document handed over on its own carries no old side.
456	The gate then stands down by name, and the pass reads the document as it stands.
457	
458	The token-identity part applies to a restructure meant to preserve content. A deliberate redesign
459	changes content by intent. Its merge stands on the green suite and the delta-scoped review pass,
460	with no token-identity demand over text the redesign meant to change.
461	
462	**The interpretation rule.** The author may state a standard out loud. Where the review sharpens it
463	past the words they used, state the sharpened form back to them, and mark it as the reviewer's own
464	reading. A standard nobody stated is never applied as though they had stated it.

466	## Phase 0 — Triage
467	
468	Before any analysis, decide whether the input is suitable.
469	
470	Check:
471	- Is this a product spec, feature doc, HLD, LLD, or design proposal?
472	- Does it describe a system with state, behavior, transitions, rather than marketing copy, vision
473	  statements, or prose with no operational content?
474	- Is there enough material to extract a model?
475	- **Does the document claim to describe a shipped system?** Then require pins: each surface naming
476	  the `file:line` that carries it. With the pins absent, every finding is conditional on the document
477	  being current. Say so, and flag any section describing a surface with no owning code or test as
478	  possibly-removed. A spec that outran a deletion will otherwise "prove" dead behaviour. Where the
479	  code is out of reach altogether, say that in one line. This happens when the document arrived on
480	  its own, or when the repository is elsewhere. Mark every finding on the already-built parts
481	  conditional, and review the document as written.
482	- **Is the input an architecture document?** That is valid input, and the review runs with the
483	  **architecture lens**. It holds seven checks, each judged at the scale the project's own kind sets.
484	  The project states its kind in a few words. Examples: a backend service, a static site, a fullstack
485	  app, a command-line tool, and a mobile app. Others: a library, a data pipeline, a skill pack, or a
486	  book. Any other kind is stated the same way. The kind decides the form each check can demand, so a skill pack and a backend
487	  service answer the placement check differently. The seven checks:
488	  - Every fact the requirements document states is owned by exactly one node.
489	  - No node stands without backing in the requirements. A node with one caller and no promised second
490	    is flagged as speculative. It waits for an answer: a named plan that turns it into a yes, or
491	    a merge back into its caller. Three questions decide whether a node stands on its own. Can it be
492	    tested by itself? Does a real second place need it? Can it and its neighbour be worked on at the
493	    same time without queuing on the same files? One "no" calls for an answer before the node stands,
494	    and the speculative-node case above is one of those. Two or more reads the node as premature.
495	  - Every seam names what crosses it and which side owns the format.
496	  - The quality budgets are stated with the place each number is measured, and each names its
497	    watcher. The watcher is the mechanical check that fails past the stated number. A decided
498	    sentence naming why a person reads a budget by eye is the other form the watcher takes.
499	  - The runtime view walks every flow the requirements promise.
500	  - The placement view says where every node runs, with its load-bearing technology where one exists.
501	  - The node-growth re-ask. Each node re-answers the three fitness questions on its pins as they
502	    stand now, because a node born right and then grown carries a standing yes nobody re-reads.
503	    Co-residence in one file is the mechanical face of a failed growth answer. Read the node count
504	    per file from this document's own pin column, counting the distinct nodes whose pins name a
505	    file. Raw file size is the wrong signal for this. A file holding more than one node is read for
506	    whether its co-resident nodes each still earn their place. Record the per-file node counts with
507	    the review. That count is a ceiling: the next review reads any file whose count rose as a question
508	    about what grew. A split moves through the architecture step and its re-review.
509	
510	  Every pin is a real `file:line` citation, and a prose description fails that bar. The paired
511	  requirements document must be in view, because ownership is checkable only against the fact list it
512	  owns. Where no such document exists, ask the author for it. Where none can be produced, record
513	  the ownership check as not runnable with that reason, and run the remaining six.
514	
515	Output one of:
516	
517	`TRIAGE: PROCEED` — analyzable. State a one-line reason. Continue to the opening assessment and Phase
518	1 in this same response, with no pause.
519	
520	`TRIAGE: NEEDS_CLARIFICATION` — the document carries too little operational content. List 2–4
521	observations, then 2–3 sharp clarifying questions. Stop there and wait.
522	
523	`TRIAGE: WRONG_ARTIFACT` — a vision deck, marketing copy, a pitch, or similar. State that plainly.
524	Offer to outline what the document would need to specify to become analyzable. Stop there.

529	seconds of a review meeting.

531	Cover:
532	- What this design is trying to do, in one sentence.
533	- The biggest 1–2 things working in this document.
534	- The biggest 1–2 things that need attention.
535	- Overall confidence: ready to build, needs another iteration, needs significant rework, or unclear

578	## Phase 3 — Property analysis
579	
580	For every entity, transition, and operation, check whether the document specifies the right
581	properties.
582	
583	3a. Things that must never happen (safety):
584	- Missing invariants: properties that must hold across all operations yet go unstated.
585	- Missing preconditions and postconditions.
586	- Atomicity: multi-step operations described as single actions; observable intermediate states;
587	  failure between steps.
588	- Rollback: what state the system returns to on failure.
589	
590	3b. Things that must eventually happen (liveness):
591	- Dead-end states: states with no defined exit.
592	- Termination: async operations, retries, migrations — is eventual completion guaranteed? Timeout,
593	  fallback, circuit breaker?
594	- Silent failure masking: can a successful event silently overwrite a previous failure?
595	
596	3c. Whether the spec can actually be enforced:
597	- Spec-model mismatch: properties promised but unenforceable in the underlying system.
598	- Counterexamples: for each non-trivial property, can you construct a sequence that breaks it?
599	
600	3d. Internal consistency:
601	- Contradicting requirements that can't simultaneously hold.
602	- Spec-model contradictions: behavior specified that no actor or transition supports.
603	- Overlapping-data agreement: sometimes two clauses independently describe overlapping data, such as
604	  a count here and the counted contents there, or a list in one section and its length in another. Is
605	  their agreement stated as an invariant? Two homes for one derivable fact with no tying sentence
606	  drift apart, and the tie is the finding's proposed sentence.
607	
608	3e. Generative stress-testing — three tiers: mandatory sweeps, imaginative probes, and the class
609	lens standing alone.
610	
611	**Open `reference/stress-lenses.md` now, and read it before writing a single Phase 3e finding.** That
612	file sits in this skill's own directory, beside this one. It carries all three tiers in full: the
613	five mandatory sweeps, the imaginative probes, and the class lens. Running Phase 3e from memory

617	them; only the file states what each one asks.

619	Stress-test every operation, transition, rule, and assumption against the families of questions the

622	The tiers differ in what they owe. `reference/stress-lenses.md` states what each tier owes, beside
623	the lenses themselves, and this page keeps no second copy of it.

625	For any given operation, one or two lenses produce a real finding, and the rest read obviously fine.
626	That is expected, and the work is in the imagining. Each axis owes a finding only where one is real.
627	A mandatory sweep owes its verdict line even at a finding count of zero, and that is what "clean"
628	says. A lens that prompts no real concern produces no finding, and inventing an issue to satisfy a
629	lens is forbidden.
